'''3.''' To secure or confirm; make sure to be or to continue; give certainty or stability to: as, to ''assure'' a person’s position or possessions.
{{smaller block|This shall ''assure'' my constant loyalty.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>My penance hath not slacken’d, though my pardon
No way ''assured.''</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 739.}}}}
{{smaller block|So irresistible an authority cannot be reflected on without the most awful reverence, even by those whose piety ''assures'' its favour to them.
{{right|''H. Rogers.''}}}}
'''4.''' To free from obscurity, ambiguity, or uncertainty.
{{smaller block|<poem>So reason’s glimmering ray
Was lent, not to ''assure'' our doubtful way,
But guide us upward to a better day.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Religio Laici.}}}}
'''5.''' To embolden; make confident.
{{smaller block|And hereby we . . . shall ''assure'' our hearts before him.
{{right|1 John iii. 19.}}}}
'''6†.''' To affiance; betroth.
{{smaller block|This drudge, or diviner, laid claim to me; called me Dromio; swore I was ''assured'' to her.
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., iii. 2.}}}}
'''7.''' To insure, as against loss. ='''Syn.''' ''Insure, Assure'' (see ''insure''); to asseverate to, encourage, vouch to, warrant.

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To confide; trust.
{{smaller block|Therfore as frend fullych in me ''assure.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 680.}}}}
'''2.''' To promise; pledge one’s self. ''Chaucer.''

'''assured''' (a-shörd′), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Certain; sure; indubitable; undoubted: as, “an ''assured'' experience,” ''Bacon'', Nat. Hist.
{{smaller block|<poem>We dare not leave his fortunes,
Though most ''assured'' death hung round about us.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, i. 1.}}}}

{{RunningHeader|assurance|352|Astacidæ}}{{nop}}{{smaller block|Plight me the full ''assurance'' of your faith. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iv. 3.}}}} '''2.''' Pledge; guaranty; surety. {{smaller block|You should procure him better ''assurance'' than Bardolph; he would not take his bond and yours; he liked not the security. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 2.}}}} '''3†.''' Affiance; betrothal. {{smaller block|The day of their ''assurance'' drew nigh. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia.}}}} {{smaller block|I am sure I never courted you, nor gave you tokens That might concern ''assurance''. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Coxcomb, iii. 1.}}}} '''4.''' In ''law'', documentary evidence of the title or right of possession of property.—'''5.''' Insurance; a contract for the payment of a sum on the occurrence of a certain event, as loss or death. {{smaller block|Recent writers have sought to establish distinctions of a novel character between them [''assurance'' and ''insurance'']. One of these is that a person insures his life, his house, or his ships, and the office assures to him in each of these cases a sum of money payable in certain contingencies. Another is that ''assurance'' represents the principle and insurance the practice. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XIII. 169.}}}} '''6.''' Certain proof; clear evidence; positive demonstration; undeniable grounds for belief or trust; assuredness. {{smaller block|Whereof he hath given ''assurance'' unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead. {{right|Acts xvii. 31.}}}} {{smaller block|A form, indeed, Where every god did seem to set his seal, To give the world ''assurance'' of a man. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|I feel desires That give ''assurance'' of their own success, And that, infus’d from Heav’n, must thither tend.}} {{smaller block|{{right|''Cowper'', The Task, v.}}}} {{smaller block|A brightness, like that of the eyes of some smaller animals, which gives ''assurance'' of life, but of a life foreign and unintelligible. {{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 44.}}}} '''7.''' Firm persuasion; full confidence or trust; freedom from doubt; certain expectation; the utmost certainty. {{smaller block|Let us draw near with a true heart, in full ''assurance'' of faith. {{right|Heb. x. 22.}}}} {{smaller block|I’ll make ''assurance'' double sure, And take a bond of fate. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 1.}} There have prevailed very widely . . . among mankind the sad tradition of a lost or forfeited life of perfection and happiness, and a dim expectation or the firm ''assurance'' of a future life of perfection and happiness. {{right|''Maudsley'', Body and Will, p. 197.}}}} Especially—'''8.''' Firmness of mind; undoubting steadiness; intrepidity; courage. {{smaller block|Brave men meet danger with ''assurance''. {{right|''Knolles''.}}}} {{smaller block|He is wanting in neither personal courage, ''assurance'', nor promptitude, but he abuses these virtues by using them in the service of vice. {{right|''P. Robinson'', Under the Sun, p. 31.}}}} '''9.''' Freedom from timidity or bashfulness; laudable confidence; self-reliance. {{smaller block|Conversation with the world will give them knowledge and ''assurance''. {{right|''Locke''.}}}} {{smaller block|I have been often surprised that you, who have seen so much of the world, . . . could never yet acquire a requisite share of ''assurance''. {{right|''Goldsmith'', She Stoops to Conquer, ii.}}}} '''10.''' Excess of boldness; impudence: as, his ''assurance'' is intolerable. {{smaller block|Immoderate ''assurance'' is perfect licentiousness. {{right|''Shenstone''.}}}} {{smaller block|Upon my soul, Jack, thou art a very impudent fellow! to do you justice, I think I never saw a piece of more consummate ''assurance!'' {{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, iv. 2.}}}} '''Chamber of assurance.''' See ''chamber''.—'''Collateral assurance.''' See ''collateral''.—'''Common assurances.''' See ''common''.—'''Further assurance.''' See ''further''. ='''Syn. 2.''' ''Pledge'', etc. See ''promise''.—'''10.''' Effrontery, presumption. '''assure''' (a̤-shör′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''assured'', ppr. ''assuring''.   [< ME. ''assuren'', ''asuren'', ''asseuren'', < OF. ''aseürer'', mod. F. ''assurer'' = Pr. ''assegurar'' = Sp. ''asegurar'' = Pg. ''assegurar'' = It. ''assecurare'' (= E. ''assecure'', q. v.), < ML. ''assecurare'', assure, < L. ''ad'', to, + ''securus'' (> OF. ''segur'', ''seür''), secure, sure: see ''secure'', ''sure''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make sure or certain; convince or make confident, as by a promise, declaration, or other evidence: as, to ''assure'' a person of one’s favor or love. {{smaller block|It is idle to propose remedies before we are ''assured'' of the disease. {{right|''Swift'', Advancement of Religion.}}}} {{smaller block|’T is a vast privilege for a Christian to be ''assured'' that the Lord will do this or that individual thing for him. {{right|''C. (''b'') In ''bot.'', rising in a curve to an erect position; ascending. Also ''adsurgent''.—'''Assurgent leaves''', leaves first bent down, but rising erect toward the apex.}} '''assuringly''' (a̤-shör′ing-li), ''adv.'' In an assuring manner; in a way to give confidence. '''asswage†''', ''v.'' An old spelling of ''assuage''. '''Assyrian''' (a̤-sir′i-a̤n), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< L. ''Assyrius'', < Gr. Ἀσσύριος, pertaining to Ἀσσυρία, Assyria.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Pertaining or relating to Assyria or to its inhabitants.{{smaller|—'''Assyrian architecture''', the most important branch of the architecture of Mesopotamia, developed in Assyria during the period of its supremacy. Its chief monuments were the royal palaces, which were of enormous extent, and constructed of massive walls of sun-dried brick on great mounds of clay, of which they have now virtually become a part, owing to the disintegrating influence of time and the elements upon their friable materials. They were never more than one or two stories high, owing to the limited endurance of the unbaked bricks, and consisted chiefly of corridors and long, narrow halls, either arched over with brick or closed in with ceilings of wood, and surrounding open courts. The entrances were of imposing height and width, ornamented with colossal stone figures of winged human-headed bulls or lions, or other mythological conceptions. The interior walls were commonly lined with a revetment of soft alabaster slabs, on which were carved in low relief the remarkable series of sculptures which have preserved the record of Assyrian triumphs, character, and customs. Color in somewhat subdued tints was generally employed upon the sculptures and the wall-spaces. The temple, in Assyria, was subordinate to the palace, the opposite being the case in Babylonia.—'''Assyrian art''', one of the later branches of Mesopotamian}} art, parallel to the later Babylonian. Its most characteristic manifestation is presented in its lavish sculptured architectural decoration in low relief. In its {{smaller block|first period, culminating in the ninth century {{sc|b. c.}}, it displayed great vigor and truth in its interpretation of nature, particularly in its portrayal of animal forms. Later it suffered a decline until the close of Assyrian supremacy, toward the end of the seventh century {{sc|b. c.}} Its human figures never have the life and force of its animals, but are heavy and conventional. It is marked by great minuteness of detail, ornaments, texture of fabrics, etc., being carefully rendered. In metal-work of all kinds the Assyrian craftsmen took a high place, and they excelled also in gem-engraving.}} [[File:century v01 p0378 c3f1.png|center|340px]] {{c|{{smaller|Assyrian Sculpture.
